summary:
Paraguay has no legal gender recognition procedure in force. Trans people are not permitted to change their name or gender on official documents, so a trans visitor whose passport marker conflicts with their presentation has no domestic route to alignment.

The judiciary has yet to issue final rulings in ten lawsuits filed by trans people seeking recognition of their legal names, among them cases brought by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda that have been pending since December 2016. Both plaintiffs have taken communications to the UN Human Rights Committee under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and are awaiting a decision. A 1993 civil court case seeking to register Ramón Fidel, who had undergone gender reassignment surgery, as a woman ended without a decision because Fidel died in a traffic accident before judgment.

Two trans migrants were denied identity documents, according to Amnesty International's 2025-26 reporting on Paraguay. Asunción's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March 2025.

Discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of their hometowns into migration and sex work, according to AP reporting from September 2025.

Since 1992 the Constitution limits marriage, de facto unions and the family to one man and one woman under Articles 49 to 52, and Article 140 of the Civil Code expressly prohibits marriage between persons of the same sex. The 8 January 2018 advisory opinion of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights holds that states party to the American Convention must grant same-sex couples access to marriage; Paraguay is an OAS party and therefore bound by the ruling, but a lawsuit relying on that opinion to recognise same-sex marriage remains pending and domestic law has not been adapted. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore has no route to recognition of that relationship in Paraguay.

There is no broad anti-discrimination law. A November 2015 bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced since introduction. Limited protections exist in specific contexts: Law 5162/2014 requires that collective dormitory placement for adolescents take into account age, sexual orientation and degree of psychic development; Decree 6973 under Law 577/2016 protects women from violence without discrimination based on sexual orientation; Law 6149/2018 bars discrimination against stateless persons based on sexual orientation and gender identity; Law 6534/2020 treats sexual orientation data as sensitive personal data; and Article 28 of the Ministry of Public Defense internal rules prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation against employees.

In October 2016 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare approved Resolution 695 requiring that trans people may use their social name on medical records, medical history and forms, and that health service officials in the Integrated Networks of Health Services must treat trans patients using their identified social name. Law 7018 on Mental Health, enacted 15 November 2022, provides in Article 3 that mental-health care is governed by non-discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity and that in no case may a diagnosis be made solely on the basis of sexual choice, sexual orientation or gender identity.

In October 2017 the Government of Paraguay implemented a ban on discussion of LGBT issues within public schools, and the Minister of Education stated it might consider burning books that raise awareness about trans people.

Amnesty International's 2025-26 reporting records 37 registered feminicides in 2025 and an April 2025 bill to merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1990, with the age of consent set at 16 for homosexual conduct and 14 for heterosexual conduct. There is no official prohibition preventing entry of gays, lesbians and bisexuals into the Armed Forces and National Police, after the Chamber of Deputies in June 2010 rejected by 42 votes to 4 a bill that would have prohibited entry of homosexuals into the Public Force.

Under the Adoption Law 1136/1997, single persons of any sex may adopt regardless of marital status; the law's prohibitions cover only infectious disease, mental disorders or child-abuse records, and equal preference is given to opposite-sex marriages and de facto unions and single women.
tangentialFactors:
During the Stroessner dictatorship (1954-1989) LGBT people faced heavy persecution. In the 1 September 1959 Caso 108, police arrested and tortured 108 gay men in Asunción and made their names public, and the government publicly encouraged hatred and violence against LGBT people.

Reports of violence and discrimination against LGBT community members are described as frequent in Paraguay and often ignored by the police. The account attributes strong influence to the Catholic Church, which has opposed measures to improve LGBT lives, alongside a rise in religious fundamentalism.

Elite-level anti-LGBT rhetoric is documented: in 2017 ruling-party figure Horacio Cartes said he would 'shoot himself in the testicles' if his son married another man, later apologising to those offended, in a report that also described a push to burn books not promoting 'traditional gender ideology'.

Public opinion on same-sex marriage is low relative to other South American countries: a Pew survey conducted 26 November 2013 to 8 January 2014 found 15% support with 81% opposed, and the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 26% support. These figures measure attitudes to same-sex marriage generally, not to trans rights.

LGBT groups have organised pride parades in Asunción since 2004.

outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of the ten name-recognition lawsuits and of the Rotela and Sepúlveda communications before the UN Human Rights Committee is unresolved in this inventory; the sources record them as pending without a date of the most recent update.

Whether the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' 2018 advisory opinion has been implemented in Paraguayan domestic law is unresolved here; the inventory records the opinion as binding on Paraguay as an OAS party and a relying lawsuit as pending, without a later ruling.

The inventory contains no entry, visa, customs or border-screening rules specific to trans travellers or to gender markers on travel documents, so no assessment of entry screening is sourced.

The 37 feminicides recorded for 2025 are not broken down by whether any victim was trans, and no trans-specific killing figure with a denominator is available here; no trans-specific rate can be stated.

The fate of the November 2015 anti-discrimination bill and of the April 2025 bill to merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family is unresolved in this inventory.

The inventory does not document any trans-specific killing or patterned violence with dates and outcomes beyond the March 2025 death of the trans human-rights defender referenced through the banned commemorative event; the circumstances of that death are not sourced here.
